newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin warns U.S. of retaliation in spy case.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin warns U.S. of retaliation in spy case.

text.p: The Kremlin warned on Sunday that it would retaliate unless U.S. authorities released a retired Russian intelligence officer arrested in New York two weeks ago.

Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) spokeswoman Tatyana Samolis said a representative of the agency had discussed the case of Vladimir Galkin with the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation late last week.
"We don't intend to leave Vladimir Galkin to the mercy of fate," she told Itar-Tass news agency. "Our patience is not unlimited and an appropriate response will not be long in coming."

Moscow says Galkin was arrested on October 29 on arrival at Kennedy airport on charges of being a former Soviet intelligence officer. This was despite the fact that he had left the service in 1992 and had clearly stated his former profession in his U.S. visa application.
The case has angered the SVR which sees it as a breach of an understanding between the rival spy agencies not to persecute retired intelligence officers.

A former top officer of the now defunct KGB suggested in an article published on Sunday that former senior Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) officers might be legitimate targets for retaliation while visiting Russia.
Nikolai Leonov, who was head of the KGB Intelligence Directorate, told the English-language Moscow Tribune that many ex-CIA men were researching books in Russian archives.

"Why don't the Russian authorities arrest former CIA directors William Colby and Stansfield Turner, as well as other retired U.S. espionage officers who have actively participated in direct operations...purporting to undermine the state security of our country in the past?"

"There exist unwritten rules of this game, a gentleman's agreement," he said, adding that the CIA and KGB had kept up secret contacts even at the height of the Cold War. These rules included a ban on assassinating each others' agents.
"Let us remain gentlemen," Leonov concluded. "Let us stick to the rules and follow our codes of honour."
Samolis said that even U.S. newspapers considered Galkin's arrest to be a political act and the charges against him concocted.

"One would like to hope that given the patience and persistence of the Russian side, commonsense will win out with the U.S. authorities and Vladimir Galkin will be released without any conditions," she told Tass.
